title: The Grain Left Standing
summary: A farmer leaves a corner of his field unharvested, and his mocking neighbour learns what the birds and the dry season know.
moral: Leave something for the ground, the birds and the neighbour who comes after you.
attribution: A traditional Shona tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: Rows of golden grain holding their heads high beside a low thatched granary

sentences.text: Tafara had the best field on the highveld: rich red soil, and rain that seemed to find it first.
Each harvest, when the other farmers stripped their fields to the last stalk, Tafara walked along the edge of his and left a broad strip of grain standing.
His neighbour, Chikomo, laughed at him.
“Are your eyes tired of looking at your own harvest, that you cannot be bothered to finish it?”
he called across the boundary.
“Next year you will have nothing left to eat, and your birds will remember you fondly.”
Tafara answered politely and kept on leaving the strip.
The birds came, as birds will, and the field mice, and the insects that had nowhere else to go.
The grain gave them shade and seed, and the roots of the standing stalks held the soil when the first heavy rains came.
That year the rains came late and then all at once.
Chikomo’s bare field washed downhill in a wide brown sheet, carrying his seed and his soil with it.
Tafara’s field held.
The strip that had been left standing slowed the water, and the earth beneath it stayed where it belonged.
When the dry weeks came, the birds that had been fed in Tafara’s field moved across the farmland and picked the beetles from every crop, including Chikomo’s.
The harvest was not one man’s harvest that year; it belonged to the valley, and the valley knew who had left something for it.
Chikomo came to ask Tafara how he knew to do this.
Tafara shook his head.
“I did not know,” he said.
“My father left a strip, and my grandmother left a strip before him.
A field is not a warehouse.
It is a friend, and a friend is given something to keep.”
